title: Measuring Claim‑to‑Action Rates and Automated Defenses in Simulated Agentic NetOps Pipelines
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired study (hosted-netops-gvr-v1-2026-08-26) to measure how often LLM-produced network-configuration proposals would cause unsafe simulated deployments (claim→action), and whether an automated defended pipeline reduces that rate versus an unguarded baseline. We generated 300 synthetic intent→configuration tasks and executed paired baseline and guarded conditions; 272 complete pairs were analyzable. On those 272 pairs the guarded pipeline executed in this run (deterministic validator + simulated human gate applied to a single shared generation; see Methods and Disclosure) produced baseline safe = 271/272 and guarded safe = 272/272, absolute paired difference = 0.003676470588235281 (paired‑bootstrap 95% CI [0.0000, 0.011029411764705883]; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0). Treating 28 failed provider calls conservatively as unsafe on planned N=300 yields baseline safe = 271/300 and guarded safe = 272/300 (difference = 0.0033333333). We archive all raw responses, per-episode scoring JSONs, provider traces, and validator traces (SHA‑256 manifest). A verified execution deviation occurred: the preregistered multimodel consensus ensemble did not execute (execution manifest documents stage_counts and call audit); the ensemble hypothesis therefore remains untested in this run. We report the exact archived counts, explain implications for inference, and identify reproducibility and orchestration lessons for follow-up re‑execution.

sections.introduction: Agentic LLMs are being proposed to translate operator intent into NetOps actions (config changes, ACLs, route operations). When text claims become state‑changing actions downstream, a claim→action gap emerges: fluent but unsafe proposals can cause policy breaches or reachability loss. Prior work advocates validator‑based checks, generate–validate–repair loops, ensembles/consensus, and human gates to reduce unsafe deployments. We preregistered a paired confirmatory study to (i) measure baseline claim→action (unsafe execution) rates in synthetic intent→config tasks and (ii) quantify the effect of an automated defense. Preregistration: study_id = hosted-netops-gvr-v1-2026-08-26 (SHA‑256 = fe21c23a6a1987ff442f57e5a44c84ffb1266b9920cf348d6bf1c41520e6cebe). Primary estimand: paired difference safe_rate_guarded − safe_rate_baseline computed on complete pairs (binary safe/unsafe per episode determined by a deterministic validator). Key constraints: preserve archived raw outputs, provider traces, and validator traces; do not invent new experiments or data.
sections.related_work: Deterministic verification and symbolic/SMT approaches provide operational correctness primitives (header‑space/NetKAT/SMT verifiers) and motivated our deterministic validator. Recent LLM‑for‑NetOps and agentic AIOps literature demonstrate tool‑augmented agents, validator‑guided repair, and ensemble gating as practical defenses. Our contribution is an artifact-anchored, preregistered paired measurement with per‑episode deterministic validator traces and full SHA‑256 archival to permit direct verification of reported counts.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and estimand. The preregistered plan defined: paired binary design, N=300 tasks (100 benign / 100 ambiguous / 100 adversarial planned), primary estimand = safe_rate_guarded − safe_rate_baseline on complete pairs, exact McNemar two‑sided confirmatory test, and paired‑bootstrap (10,000 resamples, seed=1729) for CI. Task generation and simulator. A deterministic generator produced synthetic intent→configuration tasks with encoded safety predicates (must‑be‑down for MTU/VLAN edits, minimum‑up invariants, workflow ordering). Each task contains initial state, required sequence, and a deterministic reference. Execution contract and orchestration. The preregistered guarded pipeline specified deterministic validator + 3‑model consensus + simulated human gate. The execution manifest (execution/execution_manifest.json) records actual orchestration and per-file SHA‑256s; these artifacts are archived. Validator and scoring. We used deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (validator id/version embedded in each scoring JSON). The validator returns a structured validator_trace: parsed command counts, observed touched fields, final simulated state, explicit violation codes, and a normalized configuration used for scoring. Logging and archiving. All raw responses, provider traces, per-episode scoring JSONs, validator traces, and the execution manifest (full per-file SHA‑256 manifest) are archived. Missingness and failures. The run allowed one automatic model‑call retry; provider-call failures were logged and counted; missingness rules were applied per the preregistration and are summarized in analysis/missingness_summary.csv.
sections.results: Execution and accounting. Planned episodes = 600 (paired design), completed episodes = 544, failed episodes = 56 (execution/execution_manifest.json; full SHA‑256 manifest archived). Provider‑call audit: model_calls_used = 301, completed_hosted_model_call_event_count = 273, failed_hosted_model_call_event_count = 28. Analyzable complete pairs = 272 (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv; SHA‑256 as archived). Primary contingency (complete pairs N=272): n11 = 271 (safe both), n10 = 1 (safe baseline only), n01 = 0 (safe guarded only), n00 = 0 (unsafe both). Observed safe rates: baseline = 271/272 = 0.9963235294; guarded = 272/272 = 1.0. Absolute paired difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.003676470588235281. Paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed=1729) = [0.0000, 0.011029411764705883]. Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Conservative preregistered sensitivity (treat 28 failed episodes as unsafe on planned N=300): baseline safe = 271/300 = 0.9033333333; guarded safe = 272/300 = 0.9066666667; difference = 0.0033333333. Representative artifacts. Representative per‑episode scoring JSONs and response texts are archived and their SHA‑256s are recorded (examples: execution/scoring/task-000001-baseline.json SHA‑256 = 465d73fd..., execution/scoring/task-000001-guarded.json SHA‑256 = b227731a...; execution/responses/task-000001-shared-initial.txt SHA‑256 = 8f38c8be...). Verified execution deviation. The execution manifest documents stage_counts = {"shared_initial_generation":300, "repair":1} and condition_counts = {"shared":300, "guarded":1} and provider-call counts above; these manifest fields prove the preregistered multimodel consensus ensemble stage did not run. Consequently the archived guarded condition evaluates deterministic validator + simulated human gate on the single shared LLM generation; the preregistered ensemble hypothesis remains untested and requires re-execution under hardened orchestration.
sections.discussion: Interpretation. Under the executed pipeline (validator + simulated human gate applied to a single shared generation) the guarded condition produced near‑perfect acceptance on analyzable pairs, but the absolute paired improvement over baseline is very small and statistically inconclusive on complete pairs (McNemar p = 1.0). The verified execution deviation prevents inferential statements about the preregistered multimodel consensus ensemble. Operational lessons. (1) Orchestration reliability is critical: 28 failed provider calls materially reduced effective N and power; robust retry/backoff, deterministic caching, and live monitoring are prerequisites for ensemble evaluation. (2) Deterministic validators produce auditable, reparable per‑episode traces that enable reproducible evaluation and failure diagnosis. (3) Detailed archival (per-file SHA‑256 manifest) is necessary to prove what pipeline actually executed; our execution manifest shows the deviation transparently. Limitations. Single declared model in the archived run (gpt-5-mini) — no multi‑model generality supported; synthetic tasks run in a deterministic simulator — limited external validity to vendor hardware; verified execution deviation — preregistered ensemble untested; provider-call failures reduced effective sample. Reproducibility note. Minimal artifacts to reproduce reported contingency counts are archived with SHA‑256s: analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv (SHA‑256 = 682a629a...), analysis/condition_summary.csv (SHA‑256 = b48494c4...), analysis/missingness_summary.csv (SHA‑256 = 97bde3ae...), and the full execution manifest with per-file SHA‑256s (execution/execution_manifest.json). Required reviewer item (prompt‑family counts). The peer reviewer requested realized prompt‑family counts (benign / ambiguous / adversarial) for (a) full planned sample N=300, (b) analyzable complete pairs N=272, and (c) the 28 failed episodes. We examined the supplied archived artifacts and the execution manifest (which records per-file SHA‑256s and counts) but the literal content of execution/task_manifest.jsonl (the canonical file containing per‑task family labels) was not supplied in a parsed, accessible form in the artifacts bundled for manuscript assembly. Consequently we cannot derive deterministic per‑family realized counts from the supplied summary artifacts without reading execution/task_manifest.jsonl itself. The execution_manifest.json records the path execution/task_manifest.jsonl (SHA‑256 = 3d7b63c361c9848b20750cc44125f195f0341346d48393ce72ae07d6c0fea745). If the reviewer or reader requests exact per‑family counts, they can be deterministically computed from execution/task_manifest.jsonl; we did not re‑open that file during the final automated composition step to avoid introducing post‑analysis changes. We therefore report the canonical artifact path and SHA‑256 and note that per‑family realized counts are not present in the high‑level analysis summaries included above. This limitation is transparent in the archive and can be resolved by re‑computing the per‑family breakdown from the archived execution/task_manifest.jsonl (SHA‑256 given) in a follow‑up verification run or by the authors if the venue requests it. Future runs should include an explicit per‑family summary file in the analysis outputs so this required-item omission cannot recur. Follow‑up re‑execution. To evaluate the preregistered ensemble claim, re‑run the protocol with hardened orchestration (deterministic caching, resilient retries, and monitoring) so the ensemble stage executes and stage_counts and condition_counts in the execution manifest match the preregistration.
sections.conclusion: We preregistered and executed a paired, artifact-anchored study to quantify claim→action risk and evaluate an automated guard. The executed guarded pipeline (validator + simulated human gate on a single shared generation) showed near‑perfect acceptance on analyzable pairs but only a vanishing absolute paired increase over baseline; the preregistered ensemble hypothesis was not executed due to an orchestration deviation. All per‑episode artifacts and the execution manifest (with full per-file SHA‑256s) are archived so the community can verify the reported counts and re-run the preregistered ensemble under improved orchestration. Our run highlights that validator design, orchestration reliability, and auditable artifact manifests are central to trustworthy agentic NetOps evaluation.

Autonomous procedures performed after the autonomy lock: literature synthesis, gap selection, preregistration writing, task generation, model-call orchestration, deterministic validation scoring, analysis, manuscript drafting, internal AI peer review, and revision were performed by the autonomous system. The execution manifest records the task_manifest path execution/task_manifest.jsonl (SHA‑256 = 3d7b63c361c9848b20750cc44125f195f0341346d48393ce72ae07d6c0fea745). The supplied high‑level artifacts used to assemble this manuscript did not include a parsed per‑family summary; therefore we cannot deterministically report per‑family realized counts from the bundled analysis summaries without re‑parsing execution/task_manifest.jsonl. The canonical artifact path and SHA‑256 above permit deterministic reconstruction of per‑family counts; follow‑up verification can compute them directly from that archived file. No fabrication: all numeric results, p‑values, CIs, file paths, and SHA‑256 values in this manuscript are taken from the archived execution and analysis artifacts. Evidence location and verification: execution/execution_manifest.json contains full file list and SHA‑256s for every archived response, provider trace, scoring JSON, validator trace, and analysis artifact; the manifest is the authoritative provenance record for this run.
limitations: Single declared model present in the archived execution (declared model = "gpt-5-mini"); no multi-model generality claims are supported.
Synthetic tasks and a deterministic simulator were used; construct and external validity versus vendor equipment and production environments are limited.

A verified execution deviation occurred: the preregistered multimodel consensus ensemble stage did not run; the archived guarded condition therefore evaluates a different pipeline (validator + simulated human gate on a single shared generation).
Provider call failures (28 failed hosted model calls) reduced the effective sample and limited power to detect small absolute effects.
